sections.COMMENTS:
The Periadriatic seismogenic source corresponds to the seismogenic part of the Periadriatic fault zone (PFZ). The PFZ is related to Adriatic â€“ Eurasian indented lithospheric contact zone since at least Miocene time. It is also the tectonic boundary between the Southern Alps with its S-directed fold-and-thrust belt and the rest of the Alps that experienced Cretaceous and Tertiary metamorphism and deformation.
Geochronological ages show no evidence for tectonic movements younger than mid-Miocene along the PFZ, except along the Giudicarie thrust system where exhumation rates have increased since the Messinian (Martin et al., 1998; MÃ¼ller et al., 2001). Analyses of geomorphological markers along the western section of the Periadriatic fault (corresponding to the Periadriatic West seismogenic source) revealed dextral offset river channels consistent with the expected faulting type along the structure (Garcia et al., 2010) and the general geodynamic conditions in the zone (e.g. Vrabec et al., 2006).
The long-term strain diminishes from the southern sectors of the Friuli plane and western Slovenia towards the Periadriatic fault, though the zones of the Periadriatic fault do exhibit higher strain values respect to the surrounding regions (Serpelloni et al., 2016). Instrumentally recorded seismic activity along the Periadriatic line is low, but this fault is one of the possible hosting structures of the 1348 earthquake, one of the strongest events in the region.
The minimum-maximum depth interval was established considering the geological conditions and seismic data (Willingshofer & Cloetingh, 2003; LÃ¼schen et al., 2004). The strike of the seismogenic source was based on on structural and geological maps (e.g. Linzer et al., 2002), while the dip of the source was based on seismic profiles from LÃ¼schen et al. (2004). The rake was inferred from regional structural geology and geodynamic settings. The slip rate was inferred considering the regional finite element modeling (Kastelic and Carafa, 2012) and geodetic strain rates (Serpelloni et al., 2016).
